newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish coalition sees polls this year.
newsitem.headline: Turkish coalition sees polls this year.

text.p: The conservative wing of Turkey's Islamist-led coalition said on Monday early elections would be held by the end of the year, despite doubts the coalition could leap political hurdles in the way of polls.
"This election will be carried out by the end of 1997," Hasan Ekinci, deputy chairman of the conservative True Path Party, told a news conference.

Necmettin Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, announced on Sunday he would step down later this month to let True Path leader Tansu Ciller head the government in the run up to early elections. He did not fix a date for polls.

However, investors were not convinced the government, badly wounded in a fight with the army over Islamist activism, could force elections. Istanbul's stock exchange, normally wary of the instability election talk brings, surged 4.51 points on Monday morning.
"The market does not believe that parliament approval for early polls this year can be secured because the legal procedures cannot be completed in time," said Hasan Soydan from Garanti Securities.

Political analysts say even government MPs may be reluctant to pass election legislation for fear of losing their seats and the many privileges, including generous pension benefits, that go with them.
One left-wing party, however, has urged early polls to settle a political crisis sparked by military demands for an anti-Islamist crackdown.
Ekinci said the two coalition parties had no specific date in mind for elections, normally due by the year 2000.
Turkish press reports said Erbakan, 70, had wanted a quick poll, but Ciller, under a shadow of corruption charges, had been seeking a date next spring.
President Suleyman Demirel, who would have a key role in any power handover, flew to Lithuania on Monday morning for a visit to the Baltic republics.
The Turkish media said Demirel may throw a spanner in the works of the planned transition after his return on Thursday.
"The president told Mrs Ciller that a handover of the prime minister's duties is not acknowleged in the constitution and that no procedure for it exists," the Hurriyet daily quoted Demirel as saying.

Turkish political tradition dictates that Erbakan first give his resignation to Demirel, an avowed secularist, who should then nominate the party leader with the most members of parliament to produce a feasible cabinet list.
Erbakan's Welfare Party is the largest grouping in parliament. Main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz would in theory be next in line for the chance to put together a government.
The government lost its absolute majority last week and now has 275 deputies in the 550-seat chamber. Two seats are vacant.

Analysts say handing power to Ciller would be an admission by Erbakan that he has lost his battle with secularist forces made up of the military, the judiciary and the mainstream opposition. He aroused the wrath of the secularist establishment earlier this year with proposals for mild Islamist reforms.
Since then, the army has demanded a return to strict secularism and Turkey's top prosecutor has filed a case with the Constitutional Court to have Welfare declared illegal.
